title: Buckets and Branches
focus: Sorting without a comparison, searching a trie with holes in the query, and the messiest BST operation.

cards.title: Counting and Bucket Sort
patterns: Linear when the range is small
cards.trigger: You need order but the values, or the counts, live in a small bounded range.
cards.recall: Write top-k-frequent with buckets from memory. Then answer: why is this O(n) when a heap solution is O(n log k), and what is the bucket array indexed by?
useWhen: Top k frequent elements or words
Sort characters by frequency
H-index, sort colors, any small fixed value range
Maximum gap, bucket by expected spacing
Anything where a comparison sort is overkill for the range
template: # Top k frequent in O(n): bucket index IS the frequency
buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]   # freq can be at most n
for f in range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1):       # highest frequency first
# Counting sort proper, values in [0, K]
for _ in range(c): arr[i] = v; i += 1
keyInsights: The bucket array is indexed by frequency, not by value. That inversion is what makes it linear
Frequency is bounded by n, so the bucket array has a known size. Without that bound this does not work
Counting sort is stable if you build prefix sums and place from the end. Say 'stable' if they ask about sorting records
cards.trap: 'The values are 64-bit integers.' The range is now astronomical, counting sort is dead, and you need the heap or Quickselect. Read the constraints before choosing.

cards.title: Trie with Wildcards
cards.trigger: Prefix structure plus a query that can match more than one character at a position.
cards.recall: Write the wildcard search from memory. Then answer the cost question: what is the worst-case complexity of a query that is all dots, and why does that make the structure still worth it?
useWhen: Add and search words with a dot wildcard
Word search II, many words on one board
Replace words with their shortest dictionary root
Prefix and suffix search, insert the reversed word too
Autocomplete with fuzzy first characters
template: for ch in w: n = n.kids.setdefault(ch, Node())
return any(go(kid, i + 1) for kid in node.kids.values())
return ch in node.kids and go(node.kids[ch], i + 1)
# Board search: walk the grid and the trie together. If the child does not
# exist, the whole branch is dead, which prunes thousands of grid paths at once.

problem.name: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure

keyInsights: The dot case is a branch over existing children only, not over all 26 letters. That is why real inputs are far below the bound
For word search II, the trie prunes the grid DFS. Without it you run one DFS per word and time out
Remove a word from the trie once found, so you never report it twice and the tree shrinks as you go
cards.trap: 'Support a star matching any number of characters.' That is regex, not a trie walk, and the recursion changes shape entirely. Do not pretend it is a small edit.

cards.title: BST Insert and Delete
cards.trigger: Modifying a BST while preserving the ordering invariant.
cards.recall: Write delete from memory. Then answer the case that carries the whole problem: with two children, which node replaces the deleted one, and why is either the inorder successor or the inorder predecessor valid?
useWhen: Delete or insert a node in a BST
Trim a BST to a value range
Convert a BST to a greater-sum tree
Split a BST at a value
Any BST mutation preserving order
template: if val < node.val: node.left  = insert(node.left,  val)
return node                       # always return the subtree root
if key < node.val:   node.left  = delete(node.left,  key)
elif key > node.val: node.right = delete(node.right, key)
if not node.left:  return node.right    # 0 or 1 child
while succ.left: succ = succ.left       #   = leftmost of right subtree
keyInsights: Return the subtree root from every branch. That is what lets the parent reattach without any parent pointers
The successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, so it is the smallest value still larger than the deleted one. Order is preserved by construction
Deleting the successor afterwards is safe because it has at most one child, so it hits the easy case
cards.trap: 'Repeated deletes will unbalance it.' True, and that is why AVL and red-black trees exist. Name the rebalancing rotations even though you will not implement them.

cards.title: Minimum Path Grid
cards.trigger: A grid of costs, moves restricted to a fixed direction set, and you want the best total.
cards.recall: Write it from memory using the grid itself as the table. Then answer: which cells need special initialisation, and why can you not just write one loop with `min` over both neighbours?
useWhen: Minimum path sum, maximum path sum in a grid
Triangle minimum total, bottom-up
Dungeon game, which must run backwards
Falling path sums with three-way moves
Any grid where each cell reads from already-computed neighbours
template: if r == 0 and c == 0: continue          # start cell, cost is itself
elif r == 0: grid[r][c] += grid[r][c - 1]        # only from the left
elif c == 0: grid[r][c] += grid[r - 1][c]        # only from above
# Dungeon game runs from the END backwards, because the constraint is on the
# minimum health along the way, which is not decomposable forwards.
keyInsights: The first row and first column have only one predecessor each, so they are prefix sums, not minima
Mutating the input is O(1) space but destroys it. Always say the trade rather than doing it silently
If the objective depends on the whole suffix, like minimum health, the table must be filled backwards. Direction is part of the design
cards.trap: 'Now you can also move up and left.' The dependency graph has cycles, DP is dead, and this is Dijkstra on a grid. Recognising that switch is the real test.

cards.title: Combination Backtracking
patterns: Reuse allowed means pass i, not i+1
cards.trigger: Choose a multiset of items hitting a target, where order does not matter.
cards.recall: Write combination sum from memory. Then answer the one-character question: `go(i)` versus `go(i + 1)`, which allows reuse, and what does sorting buy you beyond aesthetics?
useWhen: Combination sum, with or without reuse
Combinations of k numbers from 1 to n
Partition into k equal-sum subsets
Palindrome partitioning
Any 'all combinations' where order does not matter
template: break                      # sorted, so everything after is too big
go(i, remaining - c)           # i, not i+1: reuse allowed
# No reuse, with duplicates in the input:
#   go(i + 1, ...)  and  if i > start and c == candidates[i-1]: continue
keyInsights: `go(i)` allows reuse of the current candidate. `go(i + 1)` forbids it. One character separates two problems
Sorting turns a `continue` into a `break`, which prunes an entire tail rather than one branch
`start` is what makes combinations rather than permutations. Without it you generate every ordering
cards.trap: 'Candidates can be negative.' The remaining-value pruning breaks completely, and the search may not even terminate. Ask about negatives before you write the break.
